Player snapshot

Making history her way

Denae Benites is an American catcher whose career connects the United States women’s national team, Banana Ball, and the inaugural Women’s Pro Baseball League season.

Benites represented the United States in 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2026. The team won the 2019 COPABE Women’s Pan-American Championship and earned silver at the 2024 Women’s Baseball World Cup.

New York selected her in the first round with the sixth overall pick in the inaugural WPBL draft. She was named the Heights’ captain and hit the first home run in league history on opening day, August 1, 2026.

Published reporting also traces her path through varsity baseball in Las Vegas, EMT and volunteer-firefighter work in Delaware, and the Loco Beach Coconuts in Banana Ball.

Public service

2026

New York

How she plays

Working with her pitcher

On September 3, 2026, Benites went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBI in New York’s 18–7 win over Los Angeles. But her contribution behind the plate offered another view of her game: she told reporters that Claire Eccles felt confident in her knuckleball, and the battery used it more as Eccles finished with three hitless innings. Benites also described resetting her own approach after a first-inning strikeout. The night showed both her offensive power and the adjustments she makes with a pitcher during a game.

Source: Cliff Corcoran, The IX Sports, September 4, 2026. Checked September 13, 2026.

Player snapshot

A career across inaugural moments

Claire Eccles is a Canadian baseball player whose career connects international competition, a barrier-breaking West Coast League appearance, and the inaugural Women’s Pro Baseball League season.

New York selected Eccles 38th overall in the inaugural WPBL draft. The league lists her as a center fielder, while its 2026 statistics show appearances at the plate and as a pitcher.

In June 2017, Eccles became the first woman to play in the collegiate West Coast League when she pitched in relief for the Victoria HarbourCats. She worked two innings against the Wenatchee AppleSox, allowing one hit, one walk, and two runs.

That appearance followed international competition with Canada and collegiate softball at the University of British Columbia. Nine years later, she joined another inaugural chapter in women’s baseball as a member of the New York Heights.

Career path

Three chapters

2014–2026

Canada

Official records identify seven national-team years, including three World Cups, the 2015 Pan American Games, the 2019 qualifier, a 2022 showcase program, and the 2026 qualifier.

2015–2019

UBC + Victoria

Four UBC softball seasons overlapped with two HarbourCats baseball seasons. Victoria retired her No. 8 in 2019 after 11 mound appearances.

2026

New York

Selected 38th overall as an outfielder, Eccles appears as No. 21 and a center fielder on the preseason roster, with both batting and pitching appearances in the league’s statistics.

How she plays

A knuckleball worth trusting

On September 3, 2026, Eccles moved from center field to the mound against Los Angeles and delivered three hitless innings with six strikeouts. She stranded two inherited runners and faced the minimum nine batters; her lone walk was erased by a double play. Catcher Denae Benites told reporters that Eccles felt confident in her knuckleball that night, so they used it frequently. The outing shows another side of her value to New York: an outfielder who can change a game from the mound.

Source: Cliff Corcoran, The IX Sports, September 4, 2026. Checked September 13, 2026.

Player snapshot

A path that kept finding baseball

Ashton Lansdell is an American infielder and captain of the Los Angeles Queens whose career connects youth and college baseball, Division I softball, six United States national-team appearances, Banana Ball, and the inaugural Women’s Pro Baseball League season.

Los Angeles selected Lansdell in the first round with the seventh overall pick in the inaugural WPBL draft. The league lists her as its No. 1 third baseman, while USA Baseball’s 2026 roster lists her as an infielder/outfielder.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that she began playing baseball at age four. She played at Wheeler High School, made Team USA at 17, and continued into Georgia Highlands College. Ole Miss describes her as the first woman to play baseball at the NJCAA level.

After an ACL injury and the COVID interruption, she moved to Division I softball at FIU and Ole Miss while continuing her national-team baseball career.

Her Banana Ball path with the Party Animals continued into a first-round WPBL selection and captaincy of the inaugural Los Angeles Queens.

How she plays

A routine she can trust

Lansdell’s 2026 hitting work with Party Animals coach Anthony Coromato centered on a simpler aim: hit the ball hard and keep the same preparation from one game to the next. She told The IX Sports that regular WPBL at-bats gave her the opportunity to understand what worked for her. Her versatility serves the same practical purpose. Although she identifies with third base, she described herself as a utility player too, and the Queens used her at third and in right field. For Lansdell, adapting to another position is a way to stay in the lineup and help the team.

Source: Madison Williams, The IX Sports, August 31, 2026. Checked September 13, 2026.

Player snapshot

Always finding a place to play

Kelsie Whitmore is an American pitcher and outfielder, captain of the San Francisco Firebells, and the first overall selection in the inaugural Women’s Pro Baseball League draft.

Her baseball path spans eight documented United States national-team seasons, independent professional baseball, Banana Ball, and now the WPBL. She is also one of the seven principal players followed in Jean Fruth’s documentary See Her Be Her.

Whitmore has spent more than a decade finding places to keep playing baseball. Her professional stops include the Sonoma Stompers, Staten Island FerryHawks, Oakland Ballers, and Savannah Bananas—environments where women rarely had a roster path.

The WPBL gives that journey a different setting: a professional league built for women. San Francisco selected Whitmore first overall, named her captain, and has used her as both a hitter and starting pitcher.

Career path

Team USA

Independent baseball

Film + exhibition

See Her Be Her

Whitmore is one of the documentary’s seven principal players and joined the Savannah Bananas in 2025.

2026

San Francisco

The first overall WPBL pick entered the inaugural season as Firebells captain and delivered the league’s first reported three-home-run game.

How she plays

Three ways to shape a game

Whitmore’s September 2, 2026 performance against Boston brought her roles together. She allowed one run over four innings, hit a three-run home run, then moved to center field and made a sliding catch to stop a sixth-inning rally. San Francisco won 8–5 and clinched the top postseason seed. Pitching, hitting and defense each mattered in the same game.

Source: Cliff Corcoran, The IX Sports, September 3, 2026. Checked September 13, 2026.

Player snapshot

Calm under pressure

Alli Schroder is a Canadian right-handed pitcher, captain of the Boston Hunters, and the fifth overall selection in the inaugural Women’s Pro Baseball League draft.

At 16, Schroder pitched the final 4 1/3 innings of Canada’s extra-inning win over the United States in the 2018 Women’s Baseball World Cup bronze-medal game. She returned to help Canada win another World Cup bronze medal in 2024.

Her path also includes becoming the first woman to sign and play in the Canadian Collegiate Baseball Conference and appearing as one of seven principal players in Jean Fruth’s documentary See Her Be Her.

Away from baseball, Schroder is a wildland firefighter and crew leader in British Columbia. Boston selected her fifth overall and named her the Hunters’ first captain—a new opportunity to lead and help shape a franchise from the ground up.

Career path

Two World Cup bronze medals bookend a national-team record that began with high-pressure innings against the United States at age 16.

Schroder’s full-time wildfire career brings a real-world perspective to pressure, preparation, and responsibility on the mound.

2026

Boston captain

The fifth overall WPBL selection became the Hunters’ first captain and an inaugural professional player.

How she plays

More than a turn on the mound

Schroder wants to contribute between pitching appearances, too. After her second start at first base in three games on September 2, 2026, she told The IX Sports that playing the field and helping at the plate were part of the two-way role she wanted. Across those two starts, she went 5-for-6 with a double. That ambition adds another dimension to Boston’s captain: a pitcher looking for more ways to help her team.

Source: Cliff Corcoran, The IX Sports, September 3, 2026. Checked September 13, 2026.
